sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Cheírōn** ​(*chiron*) — ‌Wise Centaur, ‌Teacher · ​Hand — ​belongs ​to the ​Greek tradition, ​where it ‌is catalogued ​under ​the domain ‌"Wise Centaur, ​Teacher". The ‌name means ​"Hand"[^1].

Cheírōn ‌is ​the exception ​among the ​wild **κένταυροι**: ​the immortal ​son ‌of Kronos ​who dwells ‌in a ​cave on ‌Mount ​Pelion and ‌turns raw ​princes into ‌heroes. Where ​his ​kin are ‌drunkards and ‌rapine, Homer ‌calls him ​**δικαιότατος ​Κενταύρων** — ‌the most ​just of ​centaurs. He ‌is ​the teacher: ​medicine for ‌**Asklepios**, the ​lyre and ‌the remedies ​for ​**Achilles**, the ​whole heroic ​craft for ‌Iason and ‌Herakles.[^2]

​PuniCodex restores ‌the name ​as **Cheírōn** ​and serves ‌its ‌temple at ‌[cheírōn.com](https://xn--chern-1sa78d.com). The ‌original carries ​both stress ‌and ​vowel length, ​and exactly ​one historically ‌valid Unicode ​restoration ​exists, which ​places the ‌name in ​Tier 1. ​The ​plain ASCII ‌form *chiron* ​survives as ‌a modern ​convenience imposed ‌by ​the early ‌domain-name system; ‌the restoration, ​not the ​fallback, ​is the ​form the ‌project defends ‌as philologically ​complete[^3].

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
The ​name is ‌attested in ‌Greek as ​**Χείρων**. Etymologically ​it ​means "Hand"[^1].

​The ASCII ​form *chiron* ‌survives only ​because ​the early ‌domain-name system ​could not ‌carry diacritics; ​it is ‌a ​technological compromise, ​not an ​ancient spelling. ​The Unicode ​restoration ‌**Cheírōn** recovers ​the stress ‌accent of ​the original ‌directly ​in the ‌address bar. ​The original ‌carries both ​stress ​and vowel ‌length, and ‌exactly one ‌historically valid ​Unicode ​restoration exists, ‌which places ​the name ​in Tier ‌1.

​The letter-by-letter ​transformation runs:

‌- **c** ​→ **C** ‌— C ​uppercase
​- **h** ​→ **h** ​— h ‌same
- ‌**i** ​→ **e** ‌— Epsilon ​of εί
​- **r** ‌→ ‌**í** — ‌Acute iota; ‌the tonos ​of Χείρων ‌falls ​on εί
​- **o** ​→ **r** ‌— Rho
​- ​**n** → ​**ōn** — ‌Long omega ​+ nu

​Attested ​and derived ‌spellings of ​the name:

‌- **Chiron** ​— Latin/English ‌form: ​the standard ‌anglicized spelling

‌The project ​holds the ​domain ​**cheírōn.com** (xn--chern-1sa78d.com) ​as the ‌canonical home ‌of this ​name[^2].

sections.label: Pronunciation
sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The ​reconstructed pronunciation ‌of the ‌name is ​**/kʰéː.rɔːn/** — ​Attic Greek ​Reconstruction.[^1]

Phoneme ​by phoneme:

​- **Kh-** ‌— aspirated ​k (χ), ​a hard ‌stop released ​with a ‌strong breath ​— not ‌the fricative ​of modern ​Greek
​- **-eí-** ​— long ​close ē ‌(ει), carrying ​the high ‌pitch of ​the acute ‌accent
- ​**-rōn** — ‌long open ​ō (ω) ‌with final ​n

For ​the modern ‌speaker, the ‌closest approximation ‌is: ​'KHEH-rōn' — ​long ē, ‌long ō, ​the pitch ​rising on ‌the first ​syllable

Kindred ​and historical ‌forms of ​the name:

‌- **Greek** ​— χείρ ​(kheír), 'hand' ​— the ​traditional association ‌of the ‌name, possibly ​a ‌folk etymology
​- **PIE** ​— if ‌the link ‌holds, χείρ ‌descends from ‌PIE *ǵʰésr- ​'hand' (cf. ‌Hittite keššar); ​the name's ​own derivation ​remains uncertain ‌— Beekes ​treats the ​connection cautiously

​Tier 1: ‌the ​Greek original ​Χείρων carries ​both stress ‌(the acute ​on ει) ‌and long ​vowels (ει ‌and ω). ​The restored ‌form Cheírōn ‌preserves both ​marks — ​the accent ​and the ​macron — ‌that plain ‌ASCII 'Cheiron' ​erases.

sections.label: Symbols
sections.body:
The iconography ​associated with ‌Cheírōn concentrates ‌in a small ​set of ​recurring attributes, each ​a compressed ​statement about ​the name:[^1]

- ‌**The Pelian ​Ash Spear** ​— The great ‌spear of ​ash wood that ‌Cheírōn cut ​on Pelion's ‌peak and gave ​to Peleus ​at his ​wedding — the ​same spear ​Achilles alone could ‌wield (Iliad ​16.143–144). The ‌teacher's gift that ​arms the ‌hero.
- ​**The Cave on ‌Mount Pelion** ​— His dwelling ‌and school, ​the legendary ​academy of heroes ‌where the ‌gods themselves ‌celebrated the wedding ​of Peleus ​and Thetis (Pindar, ‌Pythian 9.29–30).
​- **The ​Lyre** — The ‌instrument of ​the education ​he gave Achilles, ‌who in ​Iliad 9 (186–189) ‌is found ​in his ​hut singing the ​glories of ​heroes to ‌the lyre.
- ‌**Herbs and ​Remedies (φάρμακα)** — ‌The healing ​lore he ​taught Asklepios and ‌gave to ‌Peleus's line; ‌Achilles treats wounds ‌with remedies ​'that Cheiron gave ‌his father' ​(Iliad 4.219, ​11.831–832).
- **The ​Hydra-Poisoned Arrow** ‌— Herakles's ​stray arrow, dipped ​in the ​Lernaean hydra's venom, ‌that struck ​his knee ​and gave the ​immortal an ‌unhealable wound ​(Apollodorus, Library 2.5.4).
‌- **The ​Stars** — Zeus ‌set him ​in the ‌sky — remembered ‌as Centaurus ​or Sagittarius ​— after he ​surrendered his ​immortality and died ‌(Ovid, Fasti ‌5.379–414; Hyginus, ​Astronomica 2.38).

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
Cheírōn stands at ​the hinge of two orders: Titan-born ‌yet honored by the Olympians, ‌beast-bodied yet the very image ​of wisdom. His myths are the ​myths of transmission — what ​one generation hands to the next.[^1]

​### Son of Kronos and ​Philyra (Birth)

Kronos lay with ‌the Oceanid Philyra in the shape ​of a horse, and from ​that union was born a ‌child of double nature — half ​god, half horse: *Apollodorus, Library* ‌1.2.4. Pindar likewise names him the ​son of Philyra and Kronos, ‌making Cheírōn the **half-brother of ​Zeus** (*Pythian* 4.102–103). Abandoned by his ​mother, who in shame was ​changed into a linden tree in ​later telling, he was reared ​by Apollo and Artemis, from ‌whom he learned the arts he ​would pass on. Thus the ‌wisest of teachers begins as ​the child of deception and rejection.[^2]

‌### Tutor of the Heroes ​(The School of Pelion)

Pindar gives ‌the roll of his pupils: ​in his cave Cheírōn reared ‌**Iason**, gentle-handed **Asklepios**, whom he taught ​the craft of remedies, and ​**Achilles**, whom he fed on the ‌marrow of lions and wild ‌boars to make him fierce ‌(*Nemean* 3.43–58). Homer twice seals the ​bond: Achilles carries remedies 'that ​Cheiron gave to his father ‌in friendship' (*Iliad* 4.218–219), and is ​the man 'whom Cheiron taught, ​the most just of the centaurs' ‌— *δικαιότατος Κενταύρων* (*Iliad* 11.831–832). ​Actaeon and Herakles also passed ​through his tutelage. In Pindar's grief ‌for Hieron, the poet wishes ​Cheírōn still lived in his cave, ‌that another healer might come ​to Sicily (*Pythian* 3.1–7).

### ​The Spear for Peleus (The Gift)

​When Peleus married the sea-goddess ​Thetis, the wedding feast was held ‌on Pelion at Cheírōn's cave, ‌and the centaur gave the ​bridegroom a spear of mountain ash ‌cut from Pelion's peak (*Iliad* ​16.143–144). That spear passed to ​Achilles, and at Troy no other ‌Achaean could wield it — ‌Patroklos himself left it behind when ‌he donned Achilles's armor, 'heavy, ‌huge, and strong.' The teacher's ​gift thus runs through the whole ‌*Iliad*: it is the one ​weapon that marks the hero he ​made. The marriage it honored ​also produced the child Cheírōn ‌would raise.

### The Immortal Who ​Chose Death (The Wound and ​the Stars)

When Herakles fought ​the wild centaurs at the cave ‌of Pholos, one of his ​arrows — tipped with the hydra's ​incurable venom — struck Cheírōn's ​knee (*Apollodorus, Library* 2.5.4). The ‌poison that the great healer had ​no remedy for burned in ‌his own flesh; immortal, he could ​neither heal nor die. Sophocles ‌remembers the shaft as the ​one 'wherewith Cheiron was struck' (*Trachiniae* ‌714–716). At last he surrendered ‌his immortality and was allowed ​to die, and Zeus set him ​among the stars — Ovid ​watches the father of heroes' education ​take his place in the ‌sky (*Fasti* 5.379–414; cf. Hyginus, ‌*Astronomica* 2.38). The teacher's last lesson ​is mortality itself.

sections.label: Syncretism & Reception
sections.purpose: Cross-cultural identification, later adaptations, and interpretatio.
sections.body:
Rome ​changed Cheírōn ‌least ‌of ​all the ​Greek ​figures: ​he keeps ​his ‌name ​as **Chiron** ​in ‌Latin, ​too singular ‌to ​be ‌merged with ​any ​Italian ​power. What ​Rome ​absorbed ‌was his ​catasterism ‌— ​Latin poets ‌and ​star-cataloguers ‌fixed him ​in ‌the ​sky, debating ​whether ‌the ‌Centaurus or ‌the ​Sagittarius ​was his ‌(Ovid, ​*Fasti* ​5; Hyginus, ‌*Astronomica* ​2.38). ​In later ‌tradition ​he remains ‌the ​named ​exception among ​his ​kind: ‌Dante makes ‌him ​chief ‌of the ​centaurs ​who ‌guard the ‌violent ‌in ‌*Inferno* 12, ​still ‌'Chiron, ​who nursed ​Achilles.' ​The ‌word 'centaur' ​(κένταυρος) ​traveled ​into every ‌European ​language, ​but Cheírōn ​travels ‌as ​himself.[^1]

Within ‌the ​Greek ‌tradition, closely ​related ‌names ‌in the ​corpus ​include ​[[acheron|Achérōn]], [[achilleus|Achilleús]], ​[[adamas|Adámas]], ‌[[aer|Aḗr]], ‌[[aither|Aithḗr]], and ​[[ananke|Anánkē]].

sections.label: Cultural Legacy
sections.purpose: Modern influence, literature, art, popular culture, and contemporary practice.
sections.body: His ​name ‌lives ‌in the ​sky: ​the ​minor ​planet ​**2060 Chiron**, ‌discovered ​in ​1977 ‌between ​Saturn and ‌Uranus, ​was ‌named ​for ​him and ​gave ​its ​class ‌of ​objects — ‌the ​**centaurs**, ‌bodies ​orbiting ‌among the ​giant ‌planets ​— ​their ‌collective ‌name. Modern ‌astrology ​adopted ​him ‌as ​the emblem ​of ‌the ​**wounded ​healer**, ‌the one ​whose ‌incurable ​hurt ​becomes ​the source ​of ‌healing ‌for ​others. ‌Ancient herbalists ​named ​the ‌plant ‌**centaury** ‌(κενταύριον, ‌Centaurium) after ​the ‌centaur's ​healing ​lore. ​And the ‌old ​association ​of ​his ‌name with ​χείρ, ​the ​hand, ‌echoes ​— though ‌by ​the ‌word's ​own ‌root, not ‌by ​his ​name ​— ​in 'surgery,' ‌from ‌χειρουργία, ​'hand-work.'[^1]

sections.label: Archaeology & Material Evidence
sections.purpose: Sites, inscriptions, artifacts, and physical attestations.
sections.body: No ​great ‌temple ‌of ​Cheírōn ​is known; ​he ​is ​a ‌daimonic ​tutor, ​not ‌an ​Olympian ‌with ​a state ‌cult, ​though ​a ​cave ​above ​Portaria ‌on ​Mount ‌Pelion is ​traditionally ‌identified ​as ‌the ​Cheironeion, ‌his ​school. ​His ‌real ‌monument is ‌the ​art: ​Attic ‌black- ​and ​red-figure ‌vases ​repeatedly ​show ‌Peleus handing ​the ‌infant ​Achilles ​into ​the ​centaur's ‌arms, ‌and ​Roman ‌sarcophagi of ​the ​'education ‌of ‌Achilles' ‌(2nd–3rd ‌c. ​CE) ‌show ​him ​teaching the ​lyre. ‌The ​sculpted ​centauromachies ​— ‌the ​Olympia ​west ​pediment and ‌the ​Parthenon ‌south ​metopes ‌— ​preserve ‌the ‌wild ​centaur ​type against ​which ​his ‌justice ‌was ​defined.[^1]

sections.label: Homeric Hymns
sections.body: No ​hymn to ‌Cheírōn survives, ‌and the ​silence is ​itself the ​lesson. The ​thirty-three hymns ​of the ‌Homeric collection ​address gods ​with altars ‌— powers ​invoked to ‌come, to ​hear, and ‌to give. ​Cheírōn, though ​a son ​of Krónos, ​is mortal; ​he kept ‌no precinct, ​and so ‌no rhapsode ​ever opened ‌with 'I ​begin to ‌sing of ​Cheírōn.' What ‌the tradition ​gave him ​instead was ‌wisdom literature: ‌the Χείρωνος ‌Ὑποθῆκαι (*Precepts ​of Cheírōn*), ​a Hesiodic ‌didactic poem ​counselling the ​young Achilles, ‌known now ​only from ​fragments.[^1] The ‌nearest the ​hymnic voice ‌comes to ​him is ​a wish: ​Pindar opens ​Pythian 3 ‌longing that ‌Cheírōn, the ​son of ‌Philyra, were ​alive again ​— not ‌the invocation ‌of a ‌present power ‌but grief ​for an ‌absent one.[^2] ​His end ​explains the ​absence. Pierced ‌by Heracles' ​stray arrow, ​unable to ​die though ‌longing to, ​he ceded ​his immortality ​to Prometheus ‌and was ​released; Zeus ‌set him ​among the ‌stars.[^3] A ​god is ‌hymned because ‌he endures. ​Cheírōn chose ​an end ​— and ​became not ‌a prayer ‌but a ​constellation.

sources.citation: Hesiod, fr. 283 Merkelbach–West (the Precepts of Cheírōn).
Pindar, Pythian 3.1–5 (the wish that Cheírōn were alive).
Apollodorus, Bibliotheca 2.5.4, 2.5.11 (the wound and the cession of immortality to Prometheus).

sections.label: Epithets & Epicleses
sections.body:
Homer fixed ​Cheírōn's title ‌in a ‌single line, ​and later ​poetry is ​a commentary ​upon it. ​His 'epithets' ‌are not ​cult-titles — ​no temple ‌ever received ​them — ‌but verdicts: ​the tradition ‌keeps naming ​him by ​what he was.

​- **δικαιότατος ​Κενταύρων** (*dikaiótatos ​Kentaúrōn*) — ‌'most just ​of the ‌Centaurs'; the ​defining judgment, ‌recalled when ​Patroclus' skill ‌with healing ​herbs is ‌traced back ​through Achilles ​to Cheírōn ‌(Iliad 11.832).[^1]
‌- **Φιλλυρίδης** ‌(*Phillyrídēs*) — 'son ​of Philyra'; ​Pindar invokes ‌him by ​his mother, ​the nymph ‌who bore ​him to ​Krónos in ‌horse-shape (Pythian ​3.1).[^2]
- ‌**φίλα φρονέων** ​(*phíla phronéōn*) ​— 'with ​kindly intent'; ​Homer's phrase ‌for the ‌spirit in ​which he passed ‌his gentle ​herbs to ​the house ‌of Asclepius ‌(Iliad 4.219) ‌— justice ‌expressed as ​gentleness.[^3]
- ‌**ἐκ δικαιοτάτου ​στόματος** (*ek ​dikaiotátou stómatos*) ​— 'from ‌his most ​just mouth'; ​Pindar's description ​of the ‌smile with which ​the Centaur ​answers Apollo's ​question about ‌Cyrene (Pythian ​9).[^4]
- ‌**Κένταυρος** (*Kéntauros*) ​— 'the ‌Centaur' pure ​and simple: ‌his title ‌after death, ​when the ​catasterism tradition ​set him ​among the ‌stars in ‌honor of ​his justice.[^4]

sources.citation: Homer, Iliad 11.828–832 (most just of the Centaurs).
Homer, Iliad 4.218–219 (the herbs given with kindly intent).
Pindar, Pythian 3.1; Pythian 9.29–39.
[Eratosthenes], Catasterismi 28; Hyginus, De astronomia 2.38 (the Centaur among the stars).

sections.label: Oracle & Cult Sites
sections.body: No ​oracle ever ‌spoke for ‌Cheírōn, and ​no city ​built him ​a temple; ​his holiness ​was of ‌another kind. ​His ​dwelling was ‌the cave ​on Mount ‌Pelion — ​not a ‌sanctuary with ​treasury and ​tripod but ​a school, ​where ​the sons ‌of kings ​came to ‌learn the ​lyre, the ‌hunt, and ​the herbs. ‌Pindar grants ​the ‌cave its ​one oracular ​moment: Apollo, ‌uncertain whether ‌he may ‌love the ​huntress Cyrene, ​puts the ‌question to ​the ​Centaur, and ‌Cheírōn smiles ​and answers ​— a ‌prophecy delivered ​in a ‌schoolroom, not ​a shrine.[^1] ​Thessalian religion ​did ​surround him: ‌on Pelion ‌chosen men ​climbed in ‌fresh fleeces ​at midsummer ​to Zeus ‌Aktaios against ‌the Dog ‌Star's ‌heat, and ​the Centaur's ‌cave belonged ​to that ​sacred mountain.[^2] ​After death ‌his cult ​is stellar ​rather ​than civic ‌— no ​priesthood, but ​a constellation ​that sailors ‌steered by.[^3] ​The absence ‌of an ​oracle is ‌therefore ​exact and ‌meaningful: Cheírōn ‌does not ​reveal the ​future; he ​forms the ​men who ‌will have ‌to meet ​it.

sources.citation: Pindar, Pythian 9.29–65 (the Centaur's answer to Apollo).
Scholiast on Apollonius Rhodius, Argonautica 2.498 (the fleece-clad ascent of Pelion to Zeus Aktaios).
[Eratosthenes], Catasterismi 28 (the catasterism of the Centaur).

sections.label: Iconography
sections.body:
Ancient art ​settled early ‌on how to ‌tell Cheírōn ​from his ​wild kin, and ​held to ​it for a ​thousand years: ‌he is the ​centaur civilization ​made visible.

- ‌**The labelled ​guest at ‌the wedding** — ​on the ‌François Vase by ​Kleitias (c. ​570 BC; Florence, ​Museo Archeologico ​Nazionale 4209), ΧΙΡΩΝ ​is named ‌in paint ​among the gods ‌processing to ​the marriage of ‌Peleus and ​Thetis — the ‌union whose ​child he would ‌raise.[^1]
- ​**The civilized ​centaur** — convention ‌gives him ‌human front legs ‌and a ​draped torso where ​other centaurs ‌are bare horse ​and fury; ​over his ‌shoulder a branch ​hung with ​game marks the ‌hunting he ​taught.[^2]
- **The ‌lyre** — ​the attribute of ​the music-master; ​Attic vases ​show Peleus consigning ‌the infant ‌Achilles to his ​care, and ‌the type culminates ​in the ​great fresco from ‌the Basilica ‌of Herculaneum, ‌Cheírōn guiding the ‌boy's hand ​upon the strings ‌(Naples, MAN ​inv. 9109).[^3]
- ​**The herbs** ​— his pharmacopoeia ‌remains literary ​rather than ​figured (Iliad 4.219); ​the game-laden ‌branch and the ​staff keep ​the teacher-hunter visible ​where medicine ‌cannot be painted.[^4]
​- **The ‌star-figure** — ​Roman celestial globes ‌render him ​as the kneeling ‌Centaur at ‌the altar, as ​on the ​Farnese Atlas (Naples, ​MAN inv. ​6374): the ‌cave-school of Pelion ‌translated to ​the sky.[^4]

sources.citation: Kleitias, volute-krater (the François Vase), c. 570 BC — Florence, Museo Archeologico Nazionale 4209.
LIMC III.1, s.v. 'Cheiron' (Zurich/Munich, 1986).
Fresco from the Basilica of Herculaneum — Naples, Museo Archeologico Nazionale inv. 9109.
Farnese Atlas — Naples, Museo Archeologico Nazionale inv. 6374.

sections.body: Cheírōn ​is the ‌Greek ‌answer to ​a ​question the ​centauromachy ​asks in ​stone ‌at Olympia ​and ​on ‌the Parthenon: ​can ‌nature be ​educated? ‌He is ​a ​κένταυρος — ​the ​very type ​of ‌ungoverned appetite ​— ‌who is ​instead ‌called *most ​just*. ‌That he ​is ‌Kronos's son ​and ​Zeus's half-brother ‌matters: ‌he ‌belongs to ​the ​older, Titan ‌order, ​yet serves ​the ‌new one ​by ​raising its ‌heroes, ​as if ‌the ​wild past ​could ​be redeemed ​only ‌by becoming ‌a ​teacher. His ‌unhealable ​wound ​completes the ‌thought ‌— the ‌master ‌of remedies ​cannot ‌master his ​own ​pain, and ​immortality ‌becomes not ​a ​privilege but ​a ‌sentence. That ​he ​must surrender ​deathlessness ‌to find ​release ‌is among ​the ‌most ​quietly radical ‌moments ‌in Greek ​myth: ​even an ​immortal ​may long ‌for ‌the human ​portion.[^1]
